content.text: If radioactive decay is truly random, with no way to predict when any individual nucleus will decay, how can scientists make useful predictions about radioactive substances? The answer lies in the concept of half-life. Although we cannot predict the behaviour of a single nucleus, when we have billions of nuclei (even a tiny sample contains enormous numbers of atoms), the overall behaviour becomes highly predictable through statistics. Half-life is one of the most important and practical concepts in nuclear physics, with applications ranging from medical imaging to archaeology.
The Random Nature of Radioactive Decay
It is impossible to predict exactly when any particular nucleus will decay
Each undecayed nucleus has the same constant probability of decaying in any given time interval
External conditions (temperature, pressure, chemical state) do not affect the decay rate

However, when we have a very large number of nuclei (a typical sample contains billions upon billions of atoms), the statistical average becomes extremely reliable. We can predict with great accuracy what fraction of nuclei will decay in a given time, even though we cannot say which specific nuclei will decay.
This is similar to flipping a coin. You cannot predict whether a single flip will be heads or tails, but if you flip 10,000 coins, you can confidently predict that approximately 5,000 will be heads.

The count rate is always less than the actual activity because:
The detector only captures radiation going in its direction
Some radiation may not reach the detector
The detector may not register every particle/ray that enters it
However, the count rate is proportional to the activity, so if the activity halves, the count rate also halves. This is why we can use count rate measurements to determine half-life.
When we plot the number of undecayed nuclei (or the activity, or the corrected count rate) against time, we get a characteristic
The activity halves in each equal time interval (one half-life). The curve never reaches zero.
It starts at the initial value and continuously decreases
It never reaches zero (theoretically, there are always some undecayed nuclei remaining)
The curve is steepest at the beginning and becomes more gradual over time
It has a constant half-life: the time to halve is the same regardless of the starting point on the curve
The shape is sometimes described as an "exponential decay" because the value decreases by the same fraction in each equal time interval.

One of the most famous applications of half-life is radiocarbon dating, used to determine the age of organic materials (things that were once alive).
All living organisms absorb carbon from the environment, including a small proportion of radioactive carbon-14 (
), along with the stable isotope carbon-12.
While alive, the ratio of carbon-14 to carbon-12 in the organism remains constant, because the organism continuously takes in new carbon.
When the organism dies, it stops absorbing carbon. The carbon-14 it contains continues to undergo beta decay (with a half-life of 5730 years), while the carbon-12 remains stable.

By measuring the ratio of carbon-14 to carbon-12 in a sample and comparing it to the ratio in living organisms, scientists can calculate how many half-lives have passed and therefore how long ago the organism died.
Only works for organic materials (wood, bone, cloth, etc.)
Only reliable for ages up to about 50,000-60,000 years (after about 10 half-lives, too little carbon-14 remains to measure accurately)
For much older materials (rocks, minerals), other isotopes with longer half-lives are used, such as uranium-238 (half-life of 4.5 billion years) for geological dating

Misconception 1: "After two half-lives, the entire sample has decayed"

This is incorrect. After one half-life, half remains. After two half-lives, one-quarter remains (not zero). The sample never completely decays (at least in theory). After each half-life, half of what is left decays, so there is always something remaining.
Misconception 2: "Half-life means half the nuclei decay, then the other half decay in the next half-life"
After the first half-life, half the nuclei have decayed. In the second half-life, half of the REMAINING nuclei decay (not all of them). So after two half-lives,
of the original nuclei remain, not zero.
Misconception 3: "The half-life gets longer as the sample gets smaller"

The half-life is a constant property of the isotope. It does not change regardless of how many undecayed nuclei remain. The time for the count rate to halve from 1000 to 500 is the same as the time to halve from 100 to 50.
Misconception 4: "You can measure the half-life of a single atom"

Half-life is a statistical concept that applies to large numbers of nuclei. For a single atom, you can only say there is a certain probability of it decaying in a given time. The concept of half-life only becomes meaningful with very large numbers of atoms.

Background radiation must always be subtracted from measured count rates before performing half-life calculations. Failing to do so will give incorrect values for the half-life. Background radiation is always present and does not decrease over time.

(explanation with physics reasoning) The decay curve never reaches zero because radioactive decay is a statistical process where, in each half-life, half of the remaining undecayed nuclei decay. No matter how small the number of remaining nuclei becomes, each half-life only removes half of what is left. Mathematically,
approaches zero but never equals zero. In practice, eventually the last nucleus will decay, but the smooth theoretical curve is an asymptotic curve that never touches the time axis.

Radioactive decay is random, so individual count rate readings fluctuate. This scatter in the data makes it difficult to draw a perfectly smooth curve and leads to variation in half-life readings from different parts of the graph.
